plan: In a second-price auction (winner pays second-highest bid), bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy regardless of competitors' strategies. This holds because any deviation either causes you to lose auctions you should win (bidding too low) or win auctions at a loss (bidding too high). With my value at $14, I should bid exactly $14 to maximize expected profit, letting the payment mechanism naturally protect me from overpaying.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction (winner pays the second-highest bid). In such auctions, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy regardless of the number of competitors or their strategies, since your payment doesn't depend on your own bid (only on whether you win and what the second-highest bid is). Bidding higher than value risks overpaying; bidding lower risks losing profitable wins. Therefore, I will bid exactly my value of $34.

This is a second-price sealed-bid auction. In such auctions, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do—if you bid higher than your value, you risk winning and overpaying (paying second-highest bid could exceed value only if you win due to overbidding relative to value, causing losses); if you bid lower, you risk losing profitable auctions. Since payment is second-highest bid, not your own bid, there's no incentive to shade. Therefore, I will bid exactly my value of $33.
